OK. So.

I think I better explain precisely what's going on here, since a lot of people are missing the whole story since it takes more than five seconds to explain it, and that doesn't make for good clickbait.

It is actually not as dire as the situation is being played up in the media. The way the media has it, the Internet relies on a giant computer in some bunker that says, "Internet Main Computer - Do Not Touch," and we're going to hand the root password to this device over to the UN. It doesn't work that way.

Rather, what is being ceded is ICANN. This is an organization responsible for certain aspects of Internet administration, most notably IP address allocation and the DNS root. The DNS - Domain Name System - is essentially the part of the Internet that translates, say, voat.co into the actual numerical Internet address that is actually used for computers to communicate with it. You can think of it as a phone book.

There are two reasons why this is not as important as it sounds.

  1. Anyone can build their own DNS root. You could, tonight, build a DNS root in your basement. In theory it could eventually rise to be powerful enough to challenge the ICANN DNS root. Many alternative roots have been created for a variety of reasons, though few of them have gained much traction.

  2. The root is the first level of DNS labels. Let's say that you have technet.microsoft.com. This consists of the labels 'technet,' 'microsoft', and 'com.' ICANN controls the 'com' portion of this, and IIRC subcontracts out the 'microsoft' part (actually they contract out all of it IIRC, but that's a different story). Microsoft itself controls the DNS allocation of 'technet,' and anything else under microsoft.com. So in short, ICANN only controls part of the DNS. The most important part, to be sure, but there are still substantial portions of it that are under the control of private organizations.

Now, why do these sum up to being not particularly important? Simple.

ANY COUNTRY can make their own DNS root. Easily. There were precisely two choices: first, the US could hand over control of ICANN's root, or other countries would splinter the Internet when they made their own roots, or follow some other country's root for their own country (say, China, or Russia, or maybe North Korea if we're in real whacky land). The United States retains control over the favored DNS root, the ICANN root, because of inertia and doing a (relatively) decent job of keeping it running. Individual computers can swap roots by changing a couple of numbers in your setup, and maybe rebooting. It is de facto control, and that de facto control has been under attack for some time. As such, we either lose worldwide ICANN DNS root control when it splinters (which helps to make parts of the Internet much more difficult to contact, which has negative implications for us and them), or we lose ICANN root control on our terms.

The IP address allocation, done by IANA (IIRC under ICANN's leadership) is, however, a different story. Each numerical address corresponds to what is supposed to be a single server. This is no longer the case, but IP addresses are still the basic routing unit used for one computer to communicate to another across the Internet. There are two different versions of IP addresses - IPv4 and IPv6. IPv4 is the most common, but only has 4 billion theoretical addresses available (less in practice). IPv6, which is in use internally in many communication companies but not so much for end users, has hundreds of quadrillions of addresses available. IANA says who gets what pieces of these possible addresses for both IPv4 and IPv6. This is a somewhat more tricky thing, since address block allocation can cause serious problems. However, it is much more difficult to cause meaningful disruption here than it used to be, since IPv6 is rapidly growing in popularity and importance. IPv4 rules the roost, yes, but no IANA already allocated all the IPv4 blocks - the well's dry there. It's gone. They have no more IPv4 addresses to allocate. Had this been done 15 years ago then there would be strategic value to address allocation that might be used against us, but this is much more difficult at present.

However, even with address allocation, it is worth noting that no one has a gun to their head to follow IANA's dictates. If you have address collision and conflicts in the routing tables that are used to guide where to send data packets, then bad stuff happens, yes. But that shows that IANA's authority is somewhat conditional anyway, and there are ways around it. The sheer size of IPv6 address space gives IANA little reason to risk such a schism by conducting large-scale denials of IP address space to the US or most sizable or influential countries. Truth be told, I doubt that this can prevail very much in terms of strategic denial even in small countries that might have allocations blocked. They might well destroy themselves in days that way, and if that happens there is probably no going back for them.

So what is this? Convoluted? Yes. Bad? Yes, very much so. But it is not ceding control of the entire Internet to the UN. If that were the case then they'd control the central backbone routes, which are now owned by a lot of different countries and companies anyway.

There are a lot of things worth fighting that are going on with the Internet. A lot of them. This is one. But it is not the deciding battle, not by a long shot, and truth be told, in a few years it may not matter one bit anyway, at least in terms of international communication, since soon enough there may be dozens of DNS roots sprouting up just to get around this mess in the first place.
